Discrimination and Calibration

Out of fold, the selection procedure's predictions were also calibrated (slope 1.00, Brier 0.1502, ECE 0.002) with average precision 0.430; the top decile captured 25% of events at a positive predictive value of 0.53. Development cross-validation of the fixed consensus model gave AUROC 0.7057 (fold SD 0.0020). Every result below that is not labeled out of fold comes from the exposed test partition (tertiary evidence). On it, the model reached AUROC 0.7056 (95% CI 0.6964 to 0.7145) and average precision 0.429 against a 21.3% prevalence. Calibration was close to ideal: slope 0.99 (95% CI 0.96 to 1.02), calibration-in-the-large -0.01 (95% CI -0.03 to 0.01; mean predicted 21.4% vs observed 21.3%), ECE 0.003, and Brier 0.1489 (Figure 3). At the threshold of 0.207, sensitivity was 0.624, specificity 0.674, positive predictive value 0.341, and negative predictive value 0.869. Alt text: Four panels for the test partition: a receiver operating characteristic curve with AUROC 0.706; a precision-recall curve with average precision 0.429; a calibration plot whose decile points lie close to the diagonal; and a two-by-two confusion matrix at threshold 0.207.

Sensitivity Analyses

Counting the transfer band as readmissions (refit AUROC 0.7101), excluding next admissions typed ELECTIVE (refit 0.7000), restricting to nonelective index admissions (final model 0.7073), and excluding admissions reaching the 2022 end of data (final model 0.7059) left discrimination essentially unchanged. Under the 1-hour episode rule (Timing of Readmission; flow in Supplementary Table S4), the frozen final model scored 0.6977 (95% CI 0.6880 to 0.7054) and a model refit to this outcome reached 0.7019. AUROC was stable across calendar-period bands (0.693 to 0.706; Supplementary Table S1; before the correction, 0.744 to 0.856).

Same-Cohort Clinical Baselines

Out of fold on the development partitions, the selection procedure exceeded adapted LACE (0.6055) by 0.1002 (95% CI 0.0961 to 0.1041) and HOSPITAL (0.6424) by 0.0634 (95% CI 0.0607 to 0.0662; paired, descriptive), and its top decile captured 25% of events against 16% for LACE and 20% for HOSPITAL.

On test, the final model outperformed adapted LACE (0.6050) by 0.1006 (95% CI 0.0916 to 0.1098; P<.001) and HOSPITAL (0.6468) by 0.0587 (95% CI 0.0530 to 0.0644; P<.001). Refitting the score components to this cohort raised LACE to 0.6400 and HOSPITAL to 0.6592; combining the components of both without the coded items gave 0.6647, still below the model by 0.0409 (95% CI 0.0361 to 0.0456; descriptive) (Table 3). These margins compare a model built for this outcome with scores derived for other outcomes, two of whose items use coded data our model excluded; statistical significance does not establish a clinically meaningful improvement.

Timing of Readmission 271

The test partition contributed 10,117 readmissions and 1,170 deaths before readmission (30-day 272 cumulative incidence 21.2% and 2.5%). The AFT model reached Harrell C 0.6757. Daily AUROC 273 peaked on day 1 (0.836, 95% CI 0.815 to 0.854) and fell to about 0.69 by day 7 (Figure 4). The peak was 274 an artifact: 2,368 readmissions (4.7% of events) began within 1 hour of discharge, a rate of 2,368 per hour 275 against 41 to 116 per hour at every later interval. Most appeared administrative (51% internal psychiatric 276 transfers, 14% arrivals from skilled nursing, 40% with an emergency department registration before the 277 index discharge), which is consistent with, but does not confirm, continuation; because the 1-hour 278 window was derived from the data, the primary outcome was kept and the rule is a sensitivity analysis 279 (Supplementary Methods S1, Table S4). It merges admissions beginning within 1 hour of a discharge into 280 one stay, starts the 30-day window when that stay ends, excludes stays ending in death, merges continuation rows rather than scoring them as separate index admissions, and keeps the predictions made at the first discharge, a different prediction setting from the primary analysis. Under this rule the day-1 AUROC fell to 0.683 (95% CI 0.649 to 0.719), still slightly above later days but with an interval that overlaps them; discrimination was lowest in the first week (minimum 0.636) and rose to 0.673 by day 29.

Landmark AUROCs under this rule were 0.662, 0.687, and 0.711 for days 1 to 7, 8 to 14, and 15 to 30. Alt text: Line chart of AUROC by day 1 to 29 with shaded 95% bands for two outcome definitions. The primary curve starts at 0.84 on day 1 and falls to about 0.69; the sensitivity curve starts at 0.68, dips to 0.64 in the first week, and rises to 0.67 by day 29.

.

Subgroup Performance

No difference in discrimination between Black and White patients was detected (Table 4; AUROC 0.6948 vs 0.6976; difference 0.0029, 95% CI -0.0184 to 0.0237; P=.78), but the interval does not exclude differences of up to about 0.02, so this is not evidence of equivalence. Before the leak was removed, this difference had been 0.034 (P<.001), because the leaked trend was informative mainly for patients with few prior admissions, who are more often White (median prior admissions 1 vs 3). Discrimination was lower in older patients (0.6823 for ages 75 to 84 and 0.6716 for 85 or older, vs 0.7208 for 65 to 74) and rose with prior utilization, from 0.6573 (95% CI 0.6439 to 0.6695) for first admissions, 33% of the test partition, to 0.6987 for patients with 10 or more prior admissions, who formed 46% of the highest-risk decile (Figure 5, Supplementary Table S2). Within strata the White minus Black difference remained small (standardized 0.001, 95% CI -0.017 to 0.022). At the shared threshold, specificity was 0.610 for Black and 0.685 for White patients (difference 0.075, 95% CI 0.048 to 0.102; descriptive), so nonreadmitted Black patients were flagged more often. Mean predicted risk matched observed risk for Black and White patients (observed to expected 1.00 and 1.00), but the Black calibration slope was below 1 (0.921, 95% CI 0.839 to 0.999), indicating slightly too extreme risks, and risk was overestimated for the heterogeneous other or unknown group (observed to expected 0.78).

Interpretability via SHAP

The leading predictors by mean absolute SHAP value were admission frequency by recency (0.227 on the log-odds scale), abnormal laboratory rate, laboratory results (log), prior admissions in the prior 6 months, and medication administrations (Figure 6). No single feature dominated: prior utilization, laboratory status at discharge, and the intensity of medication and laboratory activity during the stay jointly carried the signal.

Clinical Utility (Exploratory)

Decision curves showed net benefit above treat-none across thresholds 0.05 to 0.40 and above treat-all from 0.08 to 0.40 (Supplementary Appendix 4). Flagging the top 10% of admissions captured 25% of readmissions at a positive predictive value of 0.53. Patients who die without readmission are nonevents, so low risk is not clinical stability. Net benefit is not evidence that use would improve care.

Discussion

Principal Findings

In 236,906 Medicare-insured admissions, the most general finding (RQ5) is that a feature which passed a documentation-based audit and patient-grouped validation encoded later admissions; it inflated AUROC by about 0.07 and created an apparent advantage for first observed admissions, a rising calendar-period gradient, and a racial discrimination gap, all of which disappeared once it was removed. A separate outcome artifact, probable administrative continuations within an hour of discharge, accounted for most of the day-1 discrimination peak. The corrected 44-feature model reached an out-of-fold AUROC of 0.706, moderate discrimination, with near-ideal calibration on the exposed test partition; its contribution is methodological, not a deployable tool. First (RQ1, RQ3), risk was carried jointly by recency-weighted prior utilization, laboratory status at discharge, and in-hospital care intensity. Second (RQ2), on the test partition the model exceeded LACE and HOSPITAL, including versions refit to this cohort, by 0.04 to 0.10 AUROC; the scores target other outcomes, so the advantage is modest and not decisive. Third (RQ4), once probable administrative continuations were separated from readmissions, discrimination was lowest in the first week and rose later in the window; no difference by race or sex was detected, but specificity was lower for Black patients, and discrimination was lower in older patients and in first admissions.

Lessons for Leakage Auditing

The leaked feature was documented as a prior 180-day window and passed the availability audit; patientgrouped validation could not expose it because the future information was present in every partition.

Inexpensive checks caught it: testing history features among first observed admissions, flagging features constant within patients, and recomputing time-windowed features from raw timestamps. The first two are screens, not proof: constancy within patients also describes legitimate unit flags, and a first-admission test cannot detect every form of future information; recomputation from raw timestamps is the decisive step; comparing stored columns with raw tables also exposed median imputation fitted on all partitions, a quieter defect that leaks only the predictor distribution but contradicts a fold-local claim. These checks do not test whether index-stay features include events after discharge, which requires event-level timestamps.

Similarly, 4.7% of outcome events were probable administrative continuations within an hour of discharge; inspecting the distribution of discharge-to-readmission gaps is a simple safeguard before any timing claim.

Comparison With Prior Work

On MIMIC-IV, our out-of-fold AUROC of 0.706 is comparable to the structured-feature report (0.696) [32] and below notes-based (0.727) [31] and multimodal (0.791) [30] reports and full-EHR deep learning elsewhere (0.75 to 0.76) [14], which differ in cohort, outcome, and validation design. We cannot exclude similar leakage in published models that engineer history features.

Clinical Interpretation (Hypotheses)

SHAP values describe the model's reliance on a feature, not causal effects. Recency-weighted prior admissions are associated with return, possibly through unmet post-discharge needs or outpatient-access barriers, so the score should be paired with additional resources, never reduced care [5]. Discrimination is weakest for first admissions, where no history exists, and in the first post-discharge week, the window that transitional interventions target; early follow-up decisions should not rest on the score alone.

Limitations

This is a single-center, retrospective, internally validated study whose case mix (73.5% of test admissions White) differs from national Medicare; no clinical-impact evidence exists. The outcome is within-system, so out-of-system readmissions are missed, and planned readmissions are included. The model family and hyperparameters were chosen during earlier development, which had evaluated models on the test partition, and were not re-selected within the outer folds, so the out-of-fold estimate is not fully independent of those choices. The test partition was used repeatedly in earlier development, and the leak itself was found only when we re-examined an earlier version's features; the present estimates follow a principled correction rather than a fresh holdout, and residual indirect influence cannot be excluded. The validation partition participated in consensus selection and set the threshold. Earlier analysis versions used the globally imputed feature table; it was rebuilt before this version. The original code of the leaked feature, recovered in a final audit, confirms the mechanism the checks inferred. Order and transfer features were extracted with a discharge-time filter in the source pipeline and spot-checked, not fully recomputed, against raw tables. The primary outcome retains probable administrative continuations (4.7% of events). Social determinants are unavailable. Bootstrap intervals do not capture retraining or reselection variability.

Conclusion

A documented history feature that encoded later admissions survived an availability audit and patientgrouped validation, inflated discrimination, and produced spurious subgroup and calendar-period findings; first-admission tests, within-patient constancy checks, and recomputation from raw timestamps exposed it and should accompany availability audits. After correction, a calibrated 44-feature model estimates 30-day within-system readmission in Medicare-insured adults with an out-of-fold AUROC of 0.706, modestly above reconstructed and refit bedside scores. External validation and prospective evaluation are required before clinical use.

S4

dated on or before discharge was lower (86.5% and 97.2%) because 11.0% and 0.4% of admissions had a value charted during the stay, which the features correctly exclude.

Index-stay features (random sample of 3,000 admissions): numeric laboratory results per admission reproduced 100.0%, the abnormal laboratory rate 100.0%, distinct laboratory test types 94.9%, and distinct order types 99.8% (spot check made before the cutoff rebuild described below). The feature stored as orders_last_6h equals late order rate multiplied by late orders (100.0%), not orders in the final 6 hours as its name suggests. Rows recorded under an admission but timestamped after discharge were rare (0.02% of laboratory and 0.06% of order rows in a sample of 20,000 admissions; median 1.8 hours after discharge for orders) and unrelated to the outcome (AUROC 0.50 and 0.50). Laboratory value features (last hemoglobin, albumin, sodium, and white cell count; maximum bilirubin) were rebuilt for every admission from the raw laboratory table, keeping a result only if both its collection time and its storage time (storetime, when the result became available) fell on or before discharge; 6,205 of 14,905,537 results (0.04%) collected before discharge were stored afterwards and are excluded. The laboratory counts (results, abnormal rate, test types, critical results) and the prescription count, which the source pipeline had taken from every row of the admission, were rebuilt for every admission under the same cutoffs; 4.0% of laboratory result counts and 22.8% of medication counts changed (mean results 167.0 to 166.7; Supplementary Appendix 1, Cutoff_Rebuild). Two features that were exact copies of others under different names (orders_first_24h, identical to orders per day; nonenglish_x_prior_admits, identical to prior admissions in 6 months) were removed from the eligible pool.

Documentation time. MIMIC-IV records when an event occurred (charttime, starttime) and when it was documented (storetime for chart and medication-administration records; pharmacy entertime for prescriptions).

The source pipeline filtered these tables on event time only. Every chart, medication-administration, and prescription feature was therefore rebuilt from the raw tables requiring both times to fall on or before discharge. Of records already filtered by event time, 3,662 of 21,614,955 medication-administration records (0.017%), 16,621 of 11,589,196 chart records for the selected items (0.143%), and 161 of 10,469,390 prescriptions (0.002%) were documented after discharge and are now excluded. Before the cutoff the recomputed final-model features reproduced the stored values for 99.3% to 100% of admissions, confirming the definitions (two eligible candidates outside the final set, incomplete-dose count and rate, reproduced 98.4% because the source parsed the incomplete-dose field differently); the cutoff changed 1.22% of values at most (per feature in Supplementary Appendix 1, Cutoff_Rebuild, which also records the v12 count rebuild).

The discharge interval was also recomputed from any earlier admission (4.2% of values changed). Order and transfer features were extracted with a discharge-time filter in the source pipeline (ordertime, transfertime, or intime on or before discharge) and were spot-checked, not fully recomputed, against raw tables; the provider order entry table carries no separate documentation time.

S12. Same-Date Readmission and Death

Registry death dates are day-granular; same-date readmission and death were resolved death-first in the primary analysis. Resolving all 66 ties (16 in test) readmission-first changed Harrell C from 0.6757 to 0.6761 and the 30-day readmission cumulative incidence from 21.2% to 21.3%.

Electronic Health Record Model in Medicare-Insured Adults

Supplementary Appendices 1 to 6 are separate files listed in the main manuscript. All values below are generated from the released results files (results_v13 and the retained v8 to v10 audit files in results_v7).

S1. Cohort, Outcome, and Continuation Band

The outcome was the first subsequent hospitalization of the same patient in the same health system beginning more than 0 and up to 30 days (day 30 inclusive) after index discharge, of any cause and irrespective of how it ended or of the insurance recorded on it. The interval Δ is the exact difference between the next admission time and the index discharge time. Next admissions with -2<Δ≤0 days (n=650; none overlaps by more than 2 days) were treated as transfers. Admissions followed by death without readmission are nonevents in the binary frame. Because MIMIC-IV is single-center, the outcome is within-system. Continuation band. Among all 50,793 outcome events, 2,368 (4.7%; 462 in the test partition) began within 1 hour of discharge, a rate of 2,368 per hour, against 44 per hour at 1 to 2 hours, 41 at 2 to 4 hours, 94 at 6 to 12 hours, and 116 at 1 to 3 days. Of these early records, 51.0% were internal transfers to or from psychiatry, 14.4% arrivals from skilled nursing, and 40.4% carried an emergency department registration that began before the index discharge; the index discharge destination was missing for 62.6%, hospice for 14.4%, and a psychiatric facility for 16.1%. By contrast, records beginning 1 to 12 hours after discharge arrived predominantly through the emergency department after a typical emergency stay, consistent with genuine early returns. These features make most early records probable administrative continuations, but they do not establish that each one is; and the 1-hour window was chosen after inspecting the data. The primary definition was therefore retained. The 1-hour sensitivity rule treats each continuation as part of the index stay. In the raw timestamps the median gap between the index discharge and the continuation was 1 minute (90th percentile 8 minutes) and the continuation lasted a median of 7.0 days (8.5% lasted beyond day 30), so timing the window from the first discharge would count hospital days as time at risk. The rule therefore merges every consecutive admission beginning within 1 hour of the previous discharge into one stay (176 stays had more than one link), starts the 30-day window at the discharge of the last link, excludes stays ending in death (285; 54 in test), as index in-hospital deaths are excluded from the cohort, and counts the next admission if it begins within that window. Features and predictions remain those of the first discharge. Of the 1,914 remaining stays, 330 (63 in test) were followed by a genuine return and remain events; simply relabeling every continuation as a nonevent would misclassify these returns (frozen-model AUROC 0.6946 under that cruder rule). Under the episode rule (9,676 test events, 20.5%), the frozen final model scores 0.6977 (95% CI 0.6880 to 0.7054) and a model refit.

S2. Partitions and Data Flow

Admissions were split 80/20 at the patient level (GroupShuffleSplit on subject_id); 10% of the development portion formed the validation partition (18,557 admissions, 7,042 patients, 3,995 events). The 5 outer selection folds span all development patients; within each outer-training fold, 3 grouped inner folds drive staged elimination with encodings refit from inner-training patients at every step; each fold's selected model is refit on its outer-training fold and scored once on its outer-evaluation fold (primary estimate); the consensus set is formed from the 5 selections; and the final model is refit on the training partition, thresholded on the validation partition, and scored once on test. The validation partition therefore participated in consensus selection.

S3. Empirical Future-Information Tests and Timestamp Audit

Among 78,419 first observed index admissions (no earlier admission in MIMIC-IV), 51.5% had a later admission. For each of the 207 candidates we compared the share of rows at the feature's modal value between patients without and with a later admission. For a feature built only from earlier encounters this test has a sharp prediction (a single fixed value for first observed admissions); for other features, such as index-stay measurements or age, differences are expected and the test is not informative. A prior-only feature should show no systematic difference; a feature fixed at one value for every patient without a later admission, but not for others, encodes the future. Only the 180-day length-of-stay trend met this criterion: it was nonzero for 44.2% of first observed admissions, every one of which had a later admission (0.0% of patients without one . had a nonzero value; AUROC 0.929 for a later admission). Thirty-day readmission was 29.8% when the trend was nonzero and 3.1% when it was zero. The trend was also identical across all admissions of every one of the 45,154 cohort patients with more than one admission (100.0%) and zero for every patient with a single admission, so it was a per-patient summary of the whole longitudinal record. A final audit recovered the original capstone code, which confirms this: for each admission it took the length of stay minus that of the patient's previous admission, averaged these differences over the patient's whole record, and attached the mean to every admission (zero for patients with one admission), with no 180-day window. Applied to the source table, it reproduces the stored values for 100% of its 244,576 admissions. The trend and the two interaction terms built from it were removed. To test whether the trend concept itself carried signal, we rebuilt it causally: the least-squares slope of length of stay across the patient's stays admitted within 180 days before, and discharged before, the index admission, followed by the index stay (0 when no such stay exists), with the same two interactions. The rebuilt trend was zero for all first observed admissions and, among the 40.6% of admissions with an earlier stay in the window, was unrelated to later admission (AUROC 0.513). Added to the final features (both sets refit in the same run) it changed development cross-validation AUROC from 0.7057 to 0.7056 and validation-partition AUROC from 0.7169 to 0.7172, so it was not added. The largest gap among the 44 final features was 0.039 (age).

Within-patient constancy. Among the 45,154 patients with more than one admission, the removed trend was constant within 100.0% of patients. Sex is constant by construction (recorded once per patient) and is a legitimate predictor; among the other final features the highest share was 81.4% for a binary unit flag.

Constancy is a screen, not evidence of leakage; it is combined with the first-admission test and recomputation from raw timestamps.

Historical audit of the source table (v8; the discharge interval was later redefined in v13, below).

Recomputation of history features from raw admission timestamps (all 244,576 cohort admissions, using only admissions before the index admission): prior admissions of any insurance 100.0%; admissions discharged in the prior 180 days 99.7%; mean whole-day length of stay of those admissions 99.8%; any prior 180-day admission with an emergency department registration 99.6%; days since the previous Medicare-insured discharge 99.99% (a fixed value whenever no earlier Medicare-insured admission exists, 100.0% agreement); and earlier Medicare-insured admissions in the prior 365 days followed by a 30-day readmission 100.0%.

Definitions that would use later admissions matched worse (for prior readmissions, counting the index admission's own outcome 67.3%, the whole record 54.1%). Several first-pass definitions did not match; each was resolved by a causal variant, and Supplementary Table S3 now gives the verified definitions.

Outpatient-record features (candidates, not in the final model) reproduced exactly as the last value dated on or before the admission time: body-mass index 100.0%, diastolic pressure 100.0%. Agreement with the last value.

S4. Missing-Data Handling

The source feature table, inherited from the capstone pipeline, had no missing values: continuous measurements that were never taken had been imputed with the median computed over all 244,576 admissions, including the test partition, and some had been zero-filled. Comparing stored columns with raw tables identified 16 median-imputed features (last creatinine, maximum creatinine, last sodium, last potassium, last white cell count, last glucose, maximum glucose, last bnp, maximum lactate, maximum inr, last bicarbonate, last magnesium, last phosphate, heart rate variability, systolic bp variability, minimum gcs) and 5 zero-filled features (creatinine change, last bun, last hemoglobin, last albumin, maximum bilirubin). All were rebuilt from raw MIMIC-IV tables with missing values preserved; true missingness ranged from 13.9% to LACE all components AUROC 0.6400, without the coded comorbidity item 0.6381; HOSPITAL all components 0.6592, without the coded procedure item 0.6573; both scores' discharge-available components together 0.6647. Uplifts of the final model over these refits were 0.0656, 0.0674, 0.0463, 0.0483, and 0.0409 (all 95% CIs excluding zero; descriptive, no P values computed; Supplementary Appendix 1). On the.

development partitions, out of fold, adapted LACE scored 0.6055 and HOSPITAL 0.6424 against 0.7057 for the selection procedure (paired uplifts 0.1002, 95% CI 0.0961 to 0.1041, and 0.0634, 95% CI 0.0607 to 0.0662). Top-decile event capture out of fold was 25% for the procedure, 16% for LACE, and 20% for HOSPITAL.

S6. Time-to-Event Detail

Events were readmission (event 1), death before readmission within 30 days (event 2; registry deaths beyond 1 year after last discharge are censored by deidentification), and administrative censoring at day 30. The AFT model used early stopping on the validation partition (best iteration 398). Daily cumulative/dynamic AUROC keeps deaths before day t among the controls (Blanche definition 2); with no censoring before day 30, the estimate is the empirical AUROC. Treating deaths as censored at death with inverse probability weighting gave nearly identical values (day 1 0.8364 vs 0.8363). Landmark models were trained on training-partition patients still at risk when each stage opens and evaluated on the test partition: primary definition 0.6867 (4,000 events among 47,672), 0.6883 (2,545 events among 43,236), 0.7103 (3,572 events among 40,375); 1-hour episode rule 0.6619, 0.6872, 0.7110 for days 1 to 7, 8 to 14, and 15 to 30.

S7. Bootstrap and Subgroup Detail

Resample counts: 1,000 for the test panel; 800 for subgroup and prior-utilization CIs; 500 for the primary outof-fold estimate, model comparisons, and daily AUROC bands; 5,000 for contrasts with P values. Intervals resample patients and their stored predictions; selection and fitting were not repeated within draws. The White vs Black contrasts resample the union of the two patient sets jointly, so a patient recorded in both groups receives the same multiplicity in both. Race strings were consolidated by substring (WHITE to White; BLACK to Black; HISPANIC or LATINO to Hispanic or Latino; ASIAN to Asian; all others, declined, or unknown to Other or unknown). Prior admissions count every earlier admission of the patient in MIMIC-IV regardless of insurance.

S8. Demonstration Prototype

The public demonstration prototype is documented as a research prototype, not a medical device. It runs an earlier development model, not the model reported here.

Clinical-Score Reconstruction and Refits Adapted LACE (van Walraven et al.): length-of-stay points by the original bands; 3 acuity points unless elective; Charlson comorbidity points from index ICD diagnoses; and prior 180-day emergency department visits capped at 4, counting only visits that led to admission (emergency department visits without admission are not in the MIMIC-IV core tables, so the score is adapted and may understate the E component). HOSPITAL (Donze et al.): hemoglobin below 12 g/dL, oncology service, sodium below 135 mmol/L, any ICD-coded procedure, nonelective admission, prior admissions in 12 months, and length of stay of 5 days or more. Recomputed scores matched the stored test scores for 99.9% (LACE) and 100.0% (HOSPITAL) of admissions. Fixed-Set Comparison and Robustness Checks 197 With both predictor sets fixed, grouped cross-validation on identical development folds gave AUROC 0.7057 198 for the 44-feature consensus set and 0.7065 for the 137-feature pool (difference -0.0008, 95% CI -0.0017 to 199 0.0001). Consensus cross-validation folds were 0.7066, 0.7033, 0.7040, 0.7056, 0.7090.

200 Post hoc robustness checks on the validation partition (not used to change the model): with the final features 201 fitted on the training partition, the fixed hyperparameters gave AUROC 0.7177; 14 alternative settings 202 (maximum depth 3 to 8, learning rate 0.03 to 0.1 with matched tree counts) gave 0.7108 to 0.7178; five further 203 seeds gave 0.7164 to 0.7174; and training-set AUROC was 0.7585. Using 10%, 50%, and 100% of training 204 patients gave 0.6799, 0.7112, and 0.7177. A model restricted to the 6 prior-utilization features of the final set 205 reached 0.6441 on validation and 0.6448 on test (one additional test evaluation; the full model's advantage on 206 test was 0.0608, 95% CI 0.0553 to 0.0660; descriptive).
